text: That night Ivan Ivanych could not sleep, for through the wall he kept hearing his brother get up, go to the plate, and take one more gooseberry. <break time="0.8s" /> He thought of all the misery hidden behind quiet, happy homes, the poverty, sickness, and suffering of the weak, which the contented simply chose not to see. <break time="0.8s" /> Behind the door of every happy man, he thought, there should stand someone with a little hammer, knocking constantly to remind him that unhappy people exist. <break time="0.8s" /> Ivan Ivanych then confessed that he, too, had once been satisfied with life, telling others that progress must come slowly and that they should be patient. <break time="0.8s" /> Then, gripping Alyohins hands, he begged him not to grow calm and contented while he was still young, but to keep doing good as long as he lived. <break time="0.8s" /> If life has any meaning, he said, it lies not in our own happiness but in something far greater and more reasonable. <break time="0.8s" /> Neither Burkin nor Alyohin was satisfied with the story, for in that elegant room, where lovely Pelageya moved quietly about, a poor clerk eating gooseberries seemed tiresome. <break time="0.8s" /> They would rather have talked about elegant people and lovely women, and at last Alyohin, sleepy after a long day of work, said good night and went downstairs. <break time="0.8s" /> Ivan Ivanych prayed for forgiveness and pulled the quilt over his head, while Burkin lay awake, troubled by the stale smell of tobacco from his friends pipe, and the rain beat against the windows all night.
